title: Number Theory Basics
description: The core ideas of divisibility, factors, parity, and primes that power maths problems

blocks.text: Number theory is the study of whole numbers and how they relate to each other. It sounds abstract, but a surprising number of coding problems reduce to a handful of these basic ideas: divisibility, factors, parity, and primes.
This topic builds the foundation. Get comfortable here and the harder maths topics, from the sieve to modular arithmetic, will feel natural.
Number theory deals only with integers, the whole numbers like -2, 0, 7, and 100. It asks questions such as which numbers divide others, which numbers are prime, and how remainders behave.
In competitive programming and interviews, these questions appear constantly, often hidden inside a problem that looks like it is about something else entirely.

items: It studies whole numbers, not fractions or decimals
Core questions: divisibility, factors, primes, remainders
Many coding problems quietly reduce to these ideas
Mastering the basics unlocks every harder maths topic

blocks.text: We say a divides b, written a | b, when b can be split into equal groups of size a with nothing left over. In other words, the remainder of b divided by a is zero.

blocks.caption: a divides b means b is an exact multiple of a, with no remainder
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406552915-754601110.png
The modulo operator, written with a percent sign in most languages, gives that remainder. So the test a | b is simply whether b % a equals 0. This one check is the workhorse of number theory.

The key tool:

The modulo operator gives the remainder. Almost every divisibility question becomes a check of whether some remainder equals zero.

A factor (or divisor) of n is a number that divides n exactly. A multiple of n is any number you get by multiplying n by an integer. They are two sides of the same coin: if a is a factor of b, then b is a multiple of a.
Factors always come in pairs. If d divides n, then n divided by d also divides n. For 36, the pairs are 1 and 36, 2 and 18, 3 and 12, and so on.

blocks.caption: Divisors pair up around the square root, so you only need to scan up to sqrt(n)
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406552916-751089728.png
This pairing is why we can find all divisors by scanning only up to the square root of n, which we will use in the next section.
Parity is just whether a number is even or odd. A number is even if it is divisible by 2, and odd otherwise. The check is n % 2.
Parity is a small idea with big uses. Many problems have a clean answer based purely on whether a count is even or odd, and toggling parity with each step is a common trick.

items: Even means divisible by 2, odd means not
The parity of a sum depends only on how many odd numbers it contains
Many puzzles turn on a simple even or odd observation

blocks.text: A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself, like 2, 3, 5, and 7. A composite has at least one other divisor, like 4, 6, and 9.
Primes are the building blocks of all integers, since every number can be written as a product of primes. Note that 1 is neither prime nor composite, and 2 is the only even prime.

items: A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself
A composite has more than two divisors
2 is the only even prime number

blocks.text: Because divisors come in pairs around the square root, we can count or list them by looping only up to sqrt(n). For each i that divides n, we get both i and n divided by i.
This runs in O(sqrt n) instead of O(n), a big speedup for large numbers.
These simple ideas are the seeds of many problems.

items: Counting or summing the divisors of a number
Deciding if a number is prime
Problems that hinge on even or odd counts
Anything that later needs GCD, LCM, primes, or modular arithmetic

blocks.text: Every other topic in this section is built on divisibility, factors, and primes. Time spent here pays off everywhere.
